Volume 14 · Chapter 10

International macro-finance

Graduate Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v14-c09

By the endSolve open-economy dynamic models with financial and exchange-rate mechanisms.

Volume14 · Chapter10

International macro-finance

Capability. Solve dated international consumption and borrowing problems, identify what risk sharing requires, price a currency position with the correct numeraire, and close a sudden-stop mechanism through domestic goods prices and foreign financing. Four original worked cases and twelve complete exercises connect these ideas to sovereign risk and global funding conditions.

Prerequisites. Use the ownership and funding distinctions in intermediaries and liquidity, the finite default game in fiscal and sovereign debt, and the marginal-utility pricing arguments in asset pricing. All examples are synthetic. Complete-market risk sharing, currency pricing and collateral-constrained borrowing are separate models with explicitly different opportunities.

A country can run a current-account deficit while its residents accumulate foreign assets, because gross asset and liability trades differ from their net balance. A currency can have a forward premium without an expected appreciation of that size. A decline in borrowing can lower a domestic collateral price and tighten borrowing further. None of those mechanisms is established by attaching an international label to a closed-economy budget.

1. Date the external claim before drawing an inference

Use a tradable good as numeraire. In a deterministic finite endowment economy let at be the country's net foreign asset position after date-t trade, measured as principal invested at that date. Positive a is a claim on foreigners; negative a is borrowing. Endowment is yt, consumption ct, and gross return Rt>0 applies from t−1 to t. With no capital, government purchases, default or valuation adjustment,

cₜ+aₜ=yₜ+Rₜaₜ₋₁;   TBₜ=yₜ−cₜ;   CAₜ=aₜ−aₜ₋₁=TBₜ+(Rₜ−1)aₜ₋₁.

The last expression includes net interest income; a trade surplus and a current-account surplus are different statements. Setting Qt=1/(R0⋯Rt) and Q−1=1, multiply the first equation by Q and sum through T. Intermediate positions cancel:

Σₜ₌₀ᵀ Qₜ(cₜ−yₜ)=a₋₁−Q_Ta_T.

This is a finite identity. Terminal liquidation aT=0 closes a finite problem; an infinite-horizon use requires a justified terminal condition and convergence. With risky claims, the payoff depends on the state, and changes in market value need not equal net financial flows. For example, a domestic-currency depreciation increases the domestic-currency value of a fixed foreign-currency liability. That is a valuation loss, not a fresh loan receipt. Gross foreign assets, gross liabilities, maturity, currency denomination and ownership must be recorded before aggregating to a.

In a two-date model it is often simpler to denote new borrowing principal by ℓ: c0=y0−D+ℓ and c1=y1−Rℓ, where D is inherited face due now. Then a0=−ℓ, while D already includes the contractual return on the inherited position. Do not add interest to D a second time. The net current loan inflow less inherited repayment is ℓ−D; calling ℓ alone the change in external liabilities confuses a new transaction with the full dated account.

2. Complete markets share states; a single bond shares dates

Consider dates0 and1 and finitely many date1 states s with probabilities πs>0 summing to one. Two countries H,F receive positive endowments of a single freely tradable good. There is no storage, production or outside asset. Each household has log ci0+βΣπslog cis, β>0. Complete markets permit a separate claim on the good in every state. An Arrow price qs is its date0 cost, so the household budget is ci0+Σqscis≤ei0+Σqseis, including any explicitly supplied initial transfer.

Planner allocation and support. For positive welfare weights λH,λF, maximize the weighted sum of utilities subject to world resources at each node. The feasible nonnegative allocation set is compact. Giving either country zero at a positive-probability node sends weighted log welfare to −∞; a positive feasible allocation exists. Thus the maximizing allocation is strictly positive and interior. Strict concavity makes it unique. At each node λH/cH=λF/cF, so each receives its constant weight share of world endowment at that node. The same reasoning for common CRRA coefficient γ>0 gives cH/cF=(λH/λF)^(1/γ).

Set qs=βπscH0/cHs. Constant country shares make this equal to βπscF0/cFs. These positive prices support each allocation globally: concavity bounds a feasible household's utility gain by its marginal-utility-weighted spending change, which is at most zero under its budget. The sum of initial transfers needed to make the chosen allocation affordable is zero because world resources clear. Without permission to redistribute initial wealth, the weights must also satisfy each country's endowment-value budget; they cannot be selected freely. The example below supports equal weights without any initial transfer.

Complete markets do not imply equal consumption across countries with different wealth weights. Nor do they eliminate shocks to total world resources. They let countries redistribute relative endowment risk through state-contingent claims. A single safe bond, by contrast, adds the same quantity to next-period consumption in every state; it cannot generally transfer resources in opposite directions across states.

Worked case1: solve both complete and bond-only equilibria

Set (β,eH0,eF0,eH,L,eH,H,eF,L,eF,H,πL)=(19/20,1,1,3/2,1/2,1/2,3/2,1/2). World resources are two at every node. Complete markets give consumption one to each country at each node, with Arrow prices (19/40,19/40). Each country's endowment and consumption cost 39/20. H exports half a unit in its high-endowment state and imports half in its low-endowment state; F takes the opposite positions. The claims have zero net supply and zero net initial transfer. The safe bond price is19/20, hence its gross return is 20/19.

Now permit only a one-period bond paying one good in both states, at price q. If H buys a units, its consumption is(1−qa,3/2+a,1/2+a); F has the reversed endowment distribution and buys its own bond position. Each objective is strictly concave on its positive-consumption interval. At a=0 its derivative is −q+β[(1/2)/(3/2)+(1/2)/(1/2)]. Therefore 19/15 makes zero holdings globally optimal for both, clearing the bond market. Since both countries face the same endowment distribution, their unique demands coincide at every positive q; zero net supply then requires both demands to be zero and selects this q. The bond-only equilibrium gross return is 15/19. This below-one real return is possible because the model has no storage technology that guarantees a return of one.

With only the bond, each consumes its own risky future endowment. The two marginal-utility SDFs are ((19/30,19/10),(19/10,19/30)); both price the traded bond, but they differ state by state. Each country's utility gain from complete-market insurance is −(19/40)log(3/4)=0.1366489844. This is a utility difference under these endowments and preferences, not a measured percentage increase in GDP.

The example also explains a spanning caveat. Equality of two SDFs on the prices of one traded payoff imposes one expectation restriction. It does not impose equality in every state. With two states, adding an independent state-contingent payoff completes the span; with many states, the number and independence of payoffs matter.

3. Currency conversion, covered parity and the risk premium

Now measure prices in currency. Et is domestic currency per unit of foreign currency; an increase is a nominal domestic depreciation. Let X=E1/E0>0. A foreign safe bond with gross foreign-currency return RF has domestic gross return RFX. A domestic nominal SDF mD>0 prices nominal payoffs, so

1=Rᴰ E[mᴰ],   1=Rᶠ E[mᴰX];
E[X]−Rᴰ/Rᶠ=−Rᴰ Cov(mᴰ,X),
E[RᶠX]−Rᴰ=−RᴰRᶠ Cov(mᴰ,X).

The second line follows by expanding E[mX]=E[m]E[X]+Cov(m,X) and using the domestic safe return. It is an exact finite-state gross-return equation. Uncovered parity E[X]=RD/RF follows if the covariance vanishes; it is not a consequence of no arbitrage alone. Jensen terms are needed when replacing gross changes by logs, so this chapter does not silently replace E[log X] with log E[X].

With unrestricted borrowing/lending at these same safe rates, no transaction costs and enforceable conversion, a forward delivery price F0 for one foreign unit at date1 must obey F0/E0=RD/RF. Buy1/RF foreign units now, invest them abroad, and finance the domestic cost E0/RF at RD; the resulting sure domestic repayment is E0RD/RF. Reverse the trade to exclude the opposite inequality. This covered-parity proof concerns the stated replicating trades. Distinct funding rates, margins, credit limits or intermediary balance-sheet costs can break its premises; Chapter9 explains why an apparent price discrepancy is not automatically a feasible arbitrage.

Converting SDFs. For any foreign-currency payoff Z, the domestic price is E[mDE1Z]. Divide by E0 to obtain its price in foreign currency: E[mDXZ]. Thus mDX is a valid foreign SDF on convertible traded payoffs. If a proposed mF also prices them, E[(mF−mDX)Z]=0 for every traded Z. When the payoffs span every state and all probabilities are positive, select each state indicator and deduce mF=mDX state by state. Without spanning, arbitrary marginal-utility SDFs need agree only on the traded span.

For consumption baskets with price indices PD,PF, define the real exchange rate Q=EPF/PD. An increase makes the domestic basket cheaper relative to the foreign basket. A household's nominal SDF is its real marginal-utility SDF multiplied by P0/P1. Complete markets therefore imply Q1/Q0=mF,real/mD,real. Under common CRRA and discounting this becomes [(CD1/CD0)/(CF1/CF0)]^γ. This strong risk-sharing restriction uses the actual baskets, preferences and spanning assumptions; it is not an unconditional relation between measured national consumption and nominal exchange rates.

Worked case2: the forward is not the expected future spot rate

In two equally likely states take (E0,mD,L,mD,H,XL,XH,πL)=(2,4/5,6/5,6/5,9/10,1/2). The domestic safe gross return is 1. The converted foreign SDF is (24/25,27/25), so RF=50/51. Mean depreciation factor is 21/20 and Cov(mD,X)=-3/100.

The covered forward is 51/25, whereas expected future spot is 21/10. The foreign bond's domestic returns are (20/17,15/17); its expected domestic excess return is 1/34. It pays poorly in the high-domestic-marginal-value state, which explains the positive compensation. Direct pricing gives E[mDRFX]=1.

This is a complete finite-state price-consistency example. Positive Arrow prices πmD and πmF satisfy currency conversion for every claim; no full monetary equilibrium determining the price levels has been asserted. Conversely, flipping the exchange-rate quotation without changing the return formula would reverse the exposure incorrectly.

The inspected pricing-kernel section of Verdelhan's author-posted exchange-rate paper provides the complete-market SDF conversion context. The finite covariance proof and numerical example here are original; they do not reproduce the paper's habit dynamics, calibration or empirical claims.

4. A globally solved sudden stop with an endogenous domestic price

Economy and timing. Dates are0,1. A unit mass of identical price-taking households receive tradable endowments y0,y1>0 and nontradable endowments n0,n1>0. Preferences are log cT0+νlog cN0+β[log cT1+νlog cN1], ν,β>0. Nontradables cannot cross the border; their price pt is in tradables. Foreign safe lending has gross return R>0. Initial foreign obligations D satisfy0≤D<y0, so a≡y0−D>0. New borrowing principal ℓ may be negative, which represents foreign saving. All debt is repaid at date1; there is no default or further borrowing then.

cT0+p₀cN0=y₀+p₀n₀−D+ℓ;
cT1+p₁cN1=y₁+p₁n₁−Rℓ;
Rℓ≤κ(y₀+p₀n₀),   0≤κ<1.

The cap limits next-date face debt to a fraction of current gross income valued at the current domestic price. It is a stipulated enforceability restriction, not an additional resource endowment. Each household takes p0 and its income collateral as fixed when choosing consumption and ℓ. Because future tradable income is deterministic and the equilibrium debt is below y1, repayment is feasible. A changed κ is an announced funding/enforcement change before date0 choices; it is not itself an estimated shock to global risk appetite.

Household optimum at fixed prices. Both budgets are linear and the borrowing cap is affine at fixed prices. Positive consumption is required. The closure of the feasible set is bounded: positive total expenditures at each date bound ℓ below and above, and positive prices bound each good. Log utility tends to −∞ at a zero-consumption boundary; a positive feasible allocation exists in the equilibrium construction below. Strict concavity therefore gives a unique global household allocation. The intratemporal conditions give pt=νcTt/cNt. If μ≥0 is the multiplier on the face-debt cap, the borrowing condition is

1/cT0−βR/cT1=Rμ,   μ[κ(y₀+p₀n₀)−Rℓ]=0.

A constrained borrower wants to shift more goods toward date0, so the left side is nonnegative. These KKT conditions are sufficient: the concave utility tangent at a candidate, after both linear budgets cancel, is Rμ times a feasible change in ℓ, which is nonpositive when the upper cap binds. Strict concavity excludes a distinct optimum. The argument holds prices fixed and does not let a household differentiate the aggregate price response as if it owned the market.

Clear nontradables and solve the fixed point. Market clearing requires cNt=nt. Budgets then imply cT0=a+ℓ and cT1=y1−Rℓ, with p0=ν(a+ℓ)/n0, p1=ν(y1−Rℓ)/n1. The unconstrained Euler solution and the equilibrium cap, when R>κν, are

ℓU=[y₁−βRa]/[R(1+β)];   B=κ[y₀+νa]/(R−κν);   ℓ*=min{ℓU,B}.

To prove this completely, ℓU lies strictly between −a and y1/R. The Euler difference G(ℓ)=1/(a+ℓ)−βR/(y1−Rℓ) is strictly decreasing, crosses zero only at ℓU, and is positive below that point. Substitution of market-clearing prices into the cap gives (R−κν)ℓ≤κ[y0+νa]. For R>κν its upper bound B is nonnegative. Thus the displayed minimum has positive consumption and satisfies feasibility and complementarity, and no other ℓ can. Set prices as above and μ=G(ℓ*)/R. The fixed-price household sufficiency proof establishes actual optimizing households at these prices, not just an aggregate accounting solution. This constructs and uniquely characterizes a symmetric competitive equilibrium within the declared model.

At κ=0 the cap forbids positive borrowing but still permits saving. If R≤κν, do not divide by R−κν: for every positive-consumption candidate ℓ>−a, κ[y0+ν(a+ℓ)]−Rℓ=κy0+Ra+(κν−R)(a+ℓ)>0. The cap is then slack and ℓ*=ℓU. A denominator approaching zero cannot create infinite equilibrium borrowing: the unconstrained consumption optimum already bounds it. The two-date log structure gives a unique equilibrium, unlike some richer collateral models with multiple equilibria.

Foreign goods and funding. Give foreign lenders date0 tradable resources W≥0 and the inherited claim D. They put KF=W+D−ℓ into an outside technology yielding RKF at date1 and receive Rℓ from the country. Require KF≥0; choose sufficient W rather than silently assuming the money appears. Their terminal resources are R(W+D). Date0 world tradables satisfy cT0+KF=y0+W. Date1 satisfies cT1+R(W+D)=y1+RKF. This covers negative ℓ as well: the domestic saver receives −Rℓ from foreigners. Nontradable goods clear separately. R is fixed by the outside technology; this is an exact small-open-economy price equilibrium, not an endogenous world-interest-rate model.

Amplification and its limits. On a strictly binding branch with R>κν, let M=y0+νa. Then ∂ℓ/∂κ=MR/(R−κν)², ∂ℓ/∂D=−κν/(R−κν), and ∂ℓ/∂R=−κM/(R−κν)². Holding the collateral price fixed would instead give ∂ℓ/∂κ=(y0+p0n0)/R=M/(R−κν). The endogenous-price response multiplies that local change by R/(R−κν)>1 when κν>0. Lower borrowing reduces tradable demand, lowers p0 and lowers the collateral value of the nontradable endowment. Nontradable output remains n0; there is no unemployment margin in this endowment model.

Worked case3: a financing reversal and real depreciation

Set (y0,y1,D,R,β,ν,n0,n1,W)=(1,2,1/2,1,1,1,1,1,3). Compare collateral fractions (1/4,1/10). The unconstrained borrowing principal is 3/4. At κ=1/4 the cap binds at 1/2; consumption is (1,3/2) and nontradable prices are(1,3/2). The multiplier is 1/3.

Tighten κ to1/10. The unique new equilibrium has 1/6 borrowing, tradable consumption (2/3,11/6) and prices(2/3,11/6). Its multiplier is 21/22. The date0 net inflow ℓ−D changes from zero to -1/3, while the trade balance changes from zero to1/3. Current tradable consumption and p0 both fall by one third. Holding the old p0=1 fixed would have predicted borrowing1/5, leaving out the extra price-induced decline of 1/30.

For the ν=1 consumption index C=√(cTcN), cost minimization gives a unit expenditure price2√p in tradables: the optimum spends equally on the two goods. If the foreign basket is the tradable, Q is proportional to1/(2√p). Thus the real depreciation factor is 1.2247448714=√(3/2), even without a change in the nominal exchange rate. At fixed foreign prices, the domestic relative basket price has fallen.

Foreign investment is3 in the baseline and 10/3 after tightening. Baseline date1 goods total5=3/2+7/2; stressed date1 goods total16/3=11/6+7/2. Foreigners receive the same3.5 terminal resources but advance less now and invest more in their outside technology. The reversal is a change in the allocation of world goods, not their creation or destruction through a loan accounting entry.

The inspected flow-collateral section of Uribe and Schmitt-Grohé's chapter12 slides distinguishes individual price taking from aggregate collateral-price feedback. The original finite log model above proves its own global optimum and equilibrium, with an explicit terminal condition and domain. Their chapter8 slides provide the nontradable-price and real-exchange-rate convention. Neither source's estimated dynamics or multiplicity results are imported into this different model.

5. Sovereign repayment risk and the global price of a state

Chapter6 priced defaultable debt with risk-neutral foreign lenders. Retain its finite repayment/default decision but let global funding prices be represented by a positive foreign tradable-good SDF m*. For next-date face d′ and repayment indicator Hs, zero-recovery price per unit face is

q(d′)=Σₛπₛm*ₛHₛ(d′)=E[m*]E[H]+Cov(m*,H).

Thus the same repayment probability can have different prices depending on when repayment occurs and how much global investors value goods then. For a positive-price, positive-face loan, its realized gross return is H/q. Pricing requires E[m*H/q]=1. Its ordinary expected return is E[H]/q, which need not equal the global safe return1/E[m*]. A risky security that pays in high-marginal-value states can have an expected return below the safe return. Conditional repayment yield1/q alone mixes the promised payoff, default losses and state pricing.

A finite decision problem with complete enumeration. Let the country have no inherited debt, current tradable income y0>0, log utility with β>0 and a finite offered face menu containing zero. At date1 it repays d′ when log(ys−d′)≥log hs, provided ys−d′>0; otherwise it defaults and consumes hs>0. Default causes a real loss ys−hs≥0 and no recovery, and ties repay. There is no further borrowing. This makes H known for every offered contract, including contracts not chosen. Foreign state prices determine every q. For each face, consumption now is y0+qd′ and continuation consumption is ys−d′ or hs according to H. Compare the resulting finite utility values with immediate exclusion, including its stated current resource loss. Choose the best; break debt-choice ties by smallest face.

Backward optimality at the terminal date and exhaustive comparison now establish global sovereign optimality over the entire menu. Creditors' discounted payoff equals the price for every contract. Domestic repayment consumption plus the foreign receipt equals ys; in default the country consumes hs, lenders receive zero and the remaining ys−hs is a real loss. Current loan proceeds are goods supplied by foreigners. The global SDF and ample lender resources are primitives: this is a small-country equilibrium conditional on global prices, not a solution of the lenders' full portfolio/endowment equilibrium.

Worked case4: global pricing changes the chosen debt menu point

Use (y0,β,yL,yH,hL,hH,πL)=(3/5,9/10,1,2,4/5,13/10,1/2) and menu (0,1/5,3/5,9/10). Immediate exclusion consumes 1/2 now and(hL,hH) later. Its utility is -0.6754978596. Terminal repayment thresholds are(1/5,7/10), including equality.

With (4/5,6/5), global safe return is one and the full menu prices are (1,1,3/5,0). Current consumption is (3/5,4/5,24/25,3/5). Total utility, in menu order, is (-0.1989093925,-0.0590541502,0.0101759139,-0.4931763028). Face3/5 is uniquely best, financed by 9/25. The country defaults in the low state and repays in the high state; terminal consumption is(4/5,7/5).

For this selected contract, E[H]=1/2 and Cov(m*,H)=1/10, so q=1/2+1/10=3/5. Realized gross returns are(0,5/3), giving ordinary mean 5/6, below the safe return one. The positive covariance makes repayment valuable insurance to the foreign pricing kernel. Direct discounted repayment is(1/2)(6/5)(3/5)=9/25, exactly the funds advanced. There is no risk-neutral expected-return condition to impose.

Now change only the external SDF to (3/5,3/5). This is a specified global-price counterfactual, not evidence that any particular real-world shock moves every pricing-kernel component downward. The safe gross return becomes 5/3, menu prices become (3/5,3/5,3/10,0), and values become (-0.1989093925,-0.1644146659,-0.1974634509,-0.4931763028). Face1/5 is now best and both terminal states repay. New proceeds are 3/25, down from9/25. All choices, including zero debt and immediate default, were rechecked; repricing only the formerly chosen contract would not establish the new policy.

The example holds terminal default costs and incomes fixed, so the changed choice comes from global state prices and current financing. In a longer horizon, a funding change also changes continuation values and hence default regions; Chapter6's backward algorithm must be rerun at all off-path states. With domestic banks holding sovereign bonds, creditor losses can simultaneously alter domestic liquidity and collateral. That link requires the ownership and funding accounts of Chapter9 rather than a verbal assertion that a spread “causes” every balance-sheet loss.

6. From a mechanism to evidence and policy

“Global financial conditions” can mean different objects: a safe discount rate, the covariance prices in m*, an intermediary's leverage capacity, a collateral fraction, or the maturity and currency composition of funding. These objects can move together but they are not interchangeable parameters. Case3 changes κ or R in an enforceable safe borrowing economy; case4 changes state-contingent foreign valuation with endogenous repayment. An observed borrowing decline does not identify which object changed.

A research design should specify the foreign disturbance, the countries or firms exposed before it, and a comparison group with a credible reason not to share its direct demand shock. Measure gross inflows and outflows, net flows, maturity, currency positions, collateral or nontradable prices and consumption separately. Conditioning on a post-shock spread can remove part of the financing channel one hopes to measure. Exchange-rate changes also revalue existing claims, so changes in debt measured in domestic currency need not be new lending.

Reserve at least one mechanism prediction before fitting the model. For case3 it might be the joint response of tradable consumption and nontradable relative prices given predetermined foreign-currency repayment; for case4 it might be repayment frequency and the price of an unchosen debt size. Report uncertainty, alternative state prices/default costs and whether the data distinguish quantity restrictions from risk compensation. A policy comparison additionally needs the funder's cost, domestic distribution and the feasible set. Capital controls, guarantees and reserve sales change somebody's claims and incentives; a reduction in a model's borrowing limit alone does not measure their welfare effects.

7. Original exercises

  1. Derive the finite external-asset identity and the trade/current-account distinction. Let a−1=−2,R0=11/10,y0=5,c0=4 and R1=1,y1=5. Impose a1=0. Compute a0, both trade and current accounts, terminal consumption and the discounted identity. Explain why inherited face and principal cannot be interchanged.
  2. Prove the complete-market log allocation and price support from Section2, including the wealth-weight restriction. In case1 replace the two future endowments by(7/4,1/4) for H and the reverse for F. Keep all other primitives. Recompute complete Arrow prices, the bond-only price and gross return, and the complete-market utility gain. Prove that zero bond holdings clear and are individually optimal.
  3. Derive the foreign SDF conversion from an arbitrary foreign-currency payoff. State exactly when it equals a specified foreign marginal-utility SDF state by state. Derive the real-exchange-rate/relative-consumption restriction under common CRRA. Use case1's incomplete-market SDFs to explain why a bond pricing equality alone is insufficient.
  4. Derive covered parity by both directions of replication and the exact gross-return covariance correction to uncovered parity. In case2 replace X by(9/10,6/5) while holding mD,E0 and probabilities fixed; reprice the foreign safe bond consistently. Compute mF,RF,the forward,mean future spot and expected domestic excess return. Explain its sign.
  5. Prove the full symmetric equilibrium of the collateral economy for R>κν: household existence and global sufficiency at fixed prices, candidate borrowing and prices, strict positivity, uniqueness and both countries' goods accounts. Explain why replacing the price-taking household constraint by the aggregate substituted constraint before optimization can change the problem.
  6. At case3's κ=1/4 point, derive ∂ℓ/∂κ and ∂ℓ/∂D and compare the former with the derivative holding collateral prices fixed. Compute the amplification factor and the derivative of current tradable consumption with respect to inherited D. State when these derivatives cease to describe the equilibrium branch.
  7. Keep case3's κ=1/4 but raise R from1 to6/5. Compute the unconstrained loan, actual principal and face repayment, both tradable consumptions and nontradable prices. Check the binding condition. Reconcile foreign investment and both date1 consumption totals using W=3. Is the borrowing decline purely a change in currency units?
  8. Analyze κ=0 and R≤κν without dividing by a zero or negative denominator. For case3 at κ=0 give borrowing, consumptions and the net inflow. For arbitrary positive-consumption candidates prove the cap is slack when R≤κν. Explain why the cap formula cannot predict infinite borrowing as R−κν tends to zero from above.
  9. Reconstruct the entire original sovereign menu, including current default, terminal ties, all contract prices, all utility values and foreign discounted receipts. Derive why the selected contract's expected ordinary return is below the safe return despite default risk. Which conclusion would fail if lenders were risk neutral at the same safe return?
  10. In the original sovereign case reverse the global SDF to(6/5,4/5), leaving probabilities,incomes,default costs and the menu fixed. Reprice every contract and solve the whole borrowing choice. For the3/5-face contract compute its repayment covariance and ordinary expected return. Reconcile the creditor's discounted payoff; do not infer the optimum by checking only that contract.
  11. A firm owns domestic nominal assets150 and owes foreign-currency debt40. Initially E=2 domestic units per foreign unit; later E=5/2. With asset values otherwise fixed compute equity before and after. What foreign-currency asset position exactly hedges this revaluation? Explain what this accounting does not establish about exports, repayment timing, default or the macroeconomic effect of a depreciation.
  12. Referee the claim: “Covered parity holds, so uncovered parity must hold; a common global factor caused the sudden stop; its nominal depreciation proves complete risk sharing failed; and a foreign guarantee restores welfare at no domestic or foreign cost.” Give five distinct corrections, a feasible identification or reserved-moment test, and an explicit ten-point grading rubric.
Complete solutions and evaluation criteria

  1. From c+a=y+Ra−1, subtract inherited principal to get CA=TB+(R−1)a−1; discounted multiplication telescopes to the stated finite identity. Here a0=5−4−(11/10)2=-6/5. The date0 trade balance is1 and current account is 4/5, because net interest is−1/5. At date1, c1=5−6/5=19/5, and TB1=CA1=6/5. With Q0=Q1=10/11, the discounted consumption-minus-endowment sum is(10/11)(−1−6/5)=−2, equal to a−1. Inherited face due at date0 is11/5; principal is2. Multiplying that face by11/10 again would charge interest twice.

  2. Strictly positive welfare weights and world resources give an interior unique log allocation. Nodewise equal weighted marginal utilities imply constant country shares; prices βπc0/cs agree across countries. Concavity and each household's valued endowment budget prove support. Arbitrary weights require balancing initial transfers unless their allocation already satisfies those budgets. In the changed symmetric example world resources remain two, so complete consumption is one and Arrow prices stay(19/40,19/40).

    The bond-only derivative at zero gives q=(19/20)[(1/2)/(7/4)+(1/2)/(1/4)]=76/35, so R=35/76. Both households face the same reversed distribution and strictly concave scalar problems; this q makes their unique optimum zero, clearing the market. Complete insurance raises each utility by −(19/40)log(7/16)=0.3926723223. Larger idiosyncratic dispersion raises both the precautionary bond price and the gain from state-contingent insurance within this no-storage example.

  3. A foreign payoff Z has domestic price E[mDE1Z], hence foreign price E[mDXZ]. Therefore the transformed SDF is valid. Equality to a specified foreign SDF follows only if their difference is orthogonal to every traded payoff; complete spanning permits each state indicator, forcing pointwise equality. Incomplete spanning generally leaves nonzero orthogonal differences. In case1 both SDFs have mean19/15 and price the same safe bond, but their two components are reversed, so equality of means does not imply equality of the vectors.

    Using mi,nom=βu′(Ci1)/u′(Ci0)·Pi0/Pi1, substitute into X=mF,nom/mD,nom and multiply by relative basket inflation. This yields Q1/Q0=mF,real/mD,real. With common CRRA it equals the domestic-to-foreign consumption-growth ratio to power γ. Different baskets, preference shifters, heterogeneous within-country marginal utilities or absent spanning change the empirical restriction; one nominal exchange-rate observation cannot test it alone.

  4. Buying1/RF foreign units and borrowing their domestic cost replicates a sure foreign unit delivered next date at domestic cost E0RD/RF. Reversing all positions excludes a price below that cost under the same trading assumptions. Expand E[mX] and use E[m]=1/RD to obtain the covariance correction; setting it to zero requires an additional restriction.

    After reversing X, mF=(18/25,36/25), E[mF]=27/25 and RF=25/27. The forward is 54/25, while expected future spot remains21/10. Cov(mD,X)=3/100, so expected domestic excess return is -1/36. The foreign bond now pays well when domestic marginal value is high; it provides insurance and can offer a lower mean return. Keeping the old foreign safe rate after changing X would violate pricing consistency.

  5. At fixed positive prices the budget-feasible closure is bounded, the cap is linear, and zero consumption has utility−∞. A positive constructed candidate therefore beats all boundary points; strict concavity gives a unique allocation. Its consumption gradients satisfy the intratemporal price ratios. Using both budgets, its concavity tangent against a competitor reduces to[1/cT0−βR/cT1]Δℓ=RμΔℓ≤0, by cap complementarity. This proves global household sufficiency.

    Nontradable clearing imposes cNt=nt, hence cT0=a+ℓ,cT1=y1−Rℓ and their stated price ratios. For R>κν the substituted cap gives ℓ≤B≥0. G is strictly decreasing on(−a,y1/R), has its sole zero at ℓU, and ℓU lies inside that interval. The minimum of ℓU and B is therefore the unique feasible complementary solution; its prices and μ support the optimizing households. The foreign technology account gives KF=W+D−ℓ≥0,cT0+KF=y0+W and cT1+R(W+D)=y1+RKF. These are goods equations, not a second utility-maximization claim about an unspecified foreign representative consumer.

    A household controls its own borrowing but takes p0 fixed. Substituting p(aggregate ℓ) and differentiating before its choice would give it control over everybody's collateral price. That is a different strategic or planner problem. Aggregate substitution here solves market consistency only after deriving individual optimality.

  6. At the baseline a=1/2,M=3/2 and R−κν=3/4. Differentiating the binding cap gives (ℓκ,ℓD,cT0,D)=(8/3,-1/3,-4/3). Holding p0=1 fixed gives ℓκ=(1+1)/1=2, so the amplification factor is 4/3. An extra unit of inherited repayment removes one direct consumption unit and also reduces new financing by1/3 at the margin. These derivatives apply on a strictly binding, positive-consumption branch. At the switch B=ℓU, distinguish directional derivatives; on a slack branch use the unconstrained Euler formula instead.

  7. With R=6/5, ℓU=[2−(6/5)(1/2)]/[(6/5)2]=7/12. The cap is (3/8)/(19/20)=15/38, smaller than that optimum. Face repayment is 9/19, exactly κ(1+p0). Tradable consumption and prices are both (17/19,29/19), and G>0 confirms a binding cap. Foreign investment is 59/19; foreigners' date1 resources areR(W+D)=21/5. Total date1 goods are2+(6/5)(59/19)=544/95, equal to29/19+21/5. This change alters the intertemporal price and feasible financing in tradable units, not merely a nominal quotation.

  8. At κ=0, ℓ≤0, while case3's unconstrained optimum is positive. Therefore (ℓ,cT0,cT1,net inflow)=(0,1/2,2,-1/2). When R≤κν, the cap slack is κy0+Ra+(κν−R)(a+ℓ), strictly positive for positive cT0=a+ℓ. Hence it cannot bind; the unconstrained optimum supplies the equilibrium. As R−κν approaches zero from above, B may diverge, but ℓ*≤ℓU<y1/R. Eventually the cap is irrelevant. Dividing by a negative denominator and retaining the same upper-bound interpretation would reverse an inequality and solve the wrong problem.

  9. At the terminal date monotonic log utility makes repayment optimal exactly for d′≤y−h, giving thresholds(1/5,7/10), with repayment at equality. Prices for all menu points are(1,1,3/5,0). Current resources are(3/5,4/5,24/25,3/5); future chosen consumptions are respectively(1,2),(4/5,9/5),(4/5,7/5),(4/5,13/10). Substitution into log c0+(9/20)[log cL+log cH] gives the four displayed values. The highest is0.0101759139 at face3/5; immediate exclusion−0.6754978596 is lower. Each current advance equals the SDF-weighted terminal creditor receipt, including zero for the no-repayment contract.

    For d′=3/5, q=E[m*]E[H]+Cov(m*,H)=1/2+1/10=3/5. Its ordinary mean gross return is(1/2)/(3/5)=5/6 but its SDF-weighted return is one. A constant m*=1 at the same safe return would price this repayment indicator at1/2 and give mean return one; the original price3/5 and low expected-return conclusion would fail. A full borrowing choice under that changed pricing kernel would again require repricing every menu point.

  10. The reversed SDF still has mean one, but low-state-only insurance values change. Menu prices are (1,1,2/5,0), current consumptions(3/5,4/5,21/25,3/5), and utility values (-0.1989093925,-0.0590541502,-0.1233554788,-0.4931763028). Face1/5 is best, with both states repaying, and immediate default remains worse. For the3/5-face contract, Cov(m*,H)=-1/10, q=2/5 and ordinary mean gross return is 5/4. Discounted principal repayment is(1/2)(4/5)(3/5)=6/25=q·(3/5), reconciling creditor pricing. The contract pays when global marginal value is low, so it requires positive ordinary risk compensation.

  11. Initial domestic liability is2·40=80, leaving equity70. The later liability is(5/2)40=100, leaving equity50, so (equity before,equity after,loss)=(70,50,20). An existing foreign asset of40 currency units exactly offsets the liability's currency revaluation, provided its face value and credit quality do not change. Acquiring that hedge is not free; its cost and financing must be recorded. Export receipts, pass-through, maturity mismatch, collateral demands and default are absent from the simple balance sheet. It cannot establish that depreciation necessarily helps or harms the whole country.

  12. Ten-point rubric, two points per domain. (1) Separate enforceable covered replication from the uncovered covariance restriction; case2 has covered parity and a nonzero expected excess return. (2) A common factor is not an identified funding shock: define predetermined exposure, timing, comparison group and plausible direct demand/productivity confounds; distinguish R,m* and κ. (3) Nominal E differs from real Q and basket marginal utilities; a complete-sharing test must state preferences, aggregation, relative price indices and traded span. (4) Gross positions, net flows, currency valuation and default transfers require separate accounts; the case3 foreign technology and Exercise11 provide concrete checks. (5) Guarantees require a funder, state-contingent fiscal resources and altered incentives; compare a fully specified feasible policy against its opportunity cost rather than call a price increase free welfare.

    A feasible test can reserve the response of nontradable relative prices and tradable consumption among borrowers with predetermined foreign-currency maturities, then compare those responses around an externally timed funding event to less-exposed borrowers while controlling for direct foreign-demand links. Predeclare which divergence from the predicted joint response would count against the collateral mechanism, document price/flow measurement and uncertainty, and test anticipation. Alternatively reserve default frequencies across states before estimating a sovereign pricing kernel. For each domain award one point for the correct mechanism/account and one for the required assumption, evidence or concrete witness. Full credit also requires a coherent test; a missing test caps the total at eight. Policy agreement without analysis earns no points.

8. Teach-back and delayed retention

Teach-back. Explain why a country needs different claims to shift consumption across dates and across states; why a covered forward is not an unconditional exchange-rate forecast; and how a drop in borrowing can reduce its own collateral support. Benchmark. A safe bond adds the same future payoff in every state, whereas Arrow claims permit offsetting state transfers. Covered parity follows a replicating portfolio, while expected currency returns contain an SDF covariance. In the collateral economy, lower tradable consumption lowers the market-clearing nontradable price and hence the permitted face debt. Creditors still supply the dated goods, and every repayment has a recipient.

One-week retrieval. Without consulting the text, derive the foreign SDF transformation; state the borrowing solution on both sides of R=κν; reconcile both dates' tradables; and explain why a defaultable claim can have mean return below the safe return. Answers. mF=mDX is a valid transformed kernel, with equality to a specified kernel requiring the appropriate span; ℓ*=min(ℓU,B) for R>κν and ℓ*=ℓU otherwise; cT0+KF=y0+W and cT1+R(W+D)=y1+RKF; positive covariance of repayment with the lender's SDF raises its price and can lower its ordinary expected return.

Next. Quantitative solution and model evaluation (planned) asks how to diagnose approximation, identification and validation errors once such mechanisms are embedded in larger models.
